report.title: Checkout failures (api-gateway 5xx up to 32.5%) caused by a too-small DB connection pool in payments v2.4.0
report.summary: Since 16:36Z, payments v2.4.0 has been returning 503s. The deploy at 16:34Z cut its DB connection pool from 50 to 5, so requests time out waiting for a connection. The errors pass up through checkout (502) to api-gateway (502), where the 5xx rate climbed from 0% to 22.5% at 16:37Z and reached 32.5% at 16:43Z. Mitigation: roll payments back to v2.3.0.
report.impact: Starting 16:37Z, 7.5%–32.5% of api-gateway requests per minute fail with 5xx (about 1,000 requests/min). The rate is trending up: 10% at 16:40, 25% at 16:42, 32.5% at 16:43. Gateway p95 latency rose from about 180ms to 4.3–4.8s. Affected users are those whose checkout/order requests reach payments authorize/capture. Payments itself has been failing 12.5%–25% of requests since 16:36Z. Requests that do succeed still see p95 latency above 4s. Data-at-risk was not checked.

root_cause.hypothesis: Payments v2.4.0 ('Refactor DB client config loading') starts with pool.max_size=5 instead of 50. At the same traffic (1,000 req/min) the 5-connection pool is fully used. Requests wait 3000ms for a connection, then fail with TimeoutError/503, and checkout and api-gateway pass the failure on as 502s.
root_cause.trigger: Deploy of payments v2.3.0 -> v2.4.0 at 2026-10-26T16:34:00Z (commit 9f3c2ab, ci-bot, 'Refactor DB client config loading')

evidence.finding: api-gateway (v1.12.3, no version change): error_rate was 0.0 from 16:09 to 16:36. It jumped to 0.225 at 16:37, then 0.075, 0.15, 0.10, 0.175, 0.25 and 0.325 at 16:43. p95 latency went from about 170–190ms to 4310–4839ms. Requests stayed flat at 1,000/min.
api-gateway, 16:00–16:44: 53 ERROR lines. 52 are 502 'upstream checkout returned 502 Bad Gateway', spread across api-gateway-1, -2 and -3. 1 is a generic 500.
Call chain: api-gateway -> checkout -> {payments, inventory}; payments -> postgres. checkout is the gateway's only dependency.
checkout (v3.8.0, unchanged): error_rate was 0.0 until 16:36, then 0.15–0.20 from 16:37 to 16:43. p95 went from about 150ms to 4308–4700ms.
checkout, 16:30–16:44: 39 ERROR lines, all 502 'upstream payments returned 503 Service Unavailable', on checkout-1, -2 and -3.
Only one deploy between 16:00 and 16:44: payments v2.3.0 -> v2.4.0 at 16:34:00Z, commit 9f3c2ab, 'Refactor DB client config loading', status succeeded.

payments: on v2.3.0, db_pool_max was 50 and db_pool_active 18, error_rate about 0, p95 about 115–127ms. From 16:34 on v2.4.0, db_pool_max is 5 and db_pool_active stays at 5 (fully used). error_rate is 0.125–0.25 from 16:36 and p95 is 4043–4336ms.

payments, 16:30–16:44: 561 lines. 67 are ERROR 503 'TimeoutError: could not acquire connection from pool (max_size=5, timeout=3000ms)', all sampled on v2.4.0. One startup line at 16:34:20Z on payments-1: 'db client initialized: pool.max_size=5 pool.timeout_ms=3000'.
inventory (v1.4.2): error_rate 0.0 except a single 0.025 blip at 16:41. p95 steady at 56–64ms. Not affected.

postgres: no metrics returned, and search_logs returned 0 log lines. Postgres health cannot be confirmed directly. Still, payments errors are pool-acquire timeouts on the client side, not DB errors, and the pool size changed with the deploy.

timeline.event: Baseline: payments v2.3.0 has db_pool_max=50, db_pool_active=18, about 0% errors. Gateway, checkout and payments are all healthy.
payments v2.3.0 -> v2.4.0 deployed (commit 9f3c2ab, 'Refactor DB client config loading'). db_pool_max drops to 5.
payments-1 logs 'db client initialized: pool.max_size=5 pool.timeout_ms=3000'.
payments error_rate reaches 25% with p95 4149ms. Pool is fully used (5/5) and connection-acquire timeouts begin.
checkout error_rate reaches 15% (502s from payments 503s). api-gateway error_rate reaches 22.5% with p95 4533ms.
Datadog alert fires: api-gateway 5xx rate is 18.4% over 5 minutes (threshold 5%).
api-gateway error_rate reaches 32.5%, the highest so far. The incident is ongoing and getting worse.

next_steps: Roll payments back from v2.4.0 to v2.3.0 now (deploy_regression runbook step 3). Do not wait for a fix-forward.

Check recovery within about 5 minutes of the rollback: payments db_pool_max back at 50, payments, checkout and api-gateway error_rate back near 0%, and p95 back to about 120ms, 150ms and 180ms respectively.

Post in the incident channel: checkout/payment requests through api-gateway are failing at up to 32.5% since 16:37Z, cause is payments v2.4.0 pool size 5 (was 50), rollback in progress. Update every 15 minutes.

Page or ticket the payments team with the evidence: deploy 9f3c2ab at 16:34Z, startup line pool.max_size=5, 67 pool-acquire TimeoutErrors, and the config diff (pool size 50 -> 5). The refactored config loading probably falls back to a default instead of reading the configured pool size.
Confirm postgres health separately. No postgres metrics or logs were available in this investigation.
Follow-up: add an alert on payments db_pool_active/db_pool_max saturation, and a pre-deploy check that compares the effective pool config against the previous version.

report.title: Checkout failures: payments v2.4.0 shrank its DB connection pool from 50 to 5, causing pool timeouts and 5xx errors at api-gateway
report.summary: api-gateway 5xx errors began at 16:37 UTC. Since then they have been between 7.5% and 32.5% per minute, and p95 latency has been about 4.5s. Nearly all of them are 502s passed up from checkout, which in turn is passing up 503s from payments. The payments deploy v2.3.0→v2.4.0 at 16:34 ('Refactor DB client config loading') started with pool.max_size=5 instead of 50. The pool has been full at 5/5 ever since, and requests fail with 'could not acquire connection from pool (timeout=3000ms)'. The fix is to roll payments back to v2.3.0.
report.impact: Starting 2026-10-26T16:37Z and still ongoing at 16:43Z: 7.5%–32.5% of public api-gateway requests fail each minute, and the rate was rising (32.5% at 16:43). Gateway p95 latency went from about 180ms to 4.3–4.8s. Checkout/order submission is affected because payment authorize/capture calls fail with 503 (payments error rate 12.5–25%, p95 about 4.1–4.3s).

root_cause.hypothesis: The DB client config refactor in payments v2.4.0 loads pool.max_size=5 where v2.3.0 had 50. Under normal load v2.3.0 kept 18 connections active, so the 5-connection pool is full. Requests wait the full 3000ms pool timeout and return 503, which checkout turns into a 502 and api-gateway passes to users.
root_cause.trigger: payments deploy v2.3.0 → v2.4.0 (commit 9f3c2ab, ci-bot, 'Refactor DB client config loading') at 2026-10-26T16:34:00Z

report.title: payments v2.4.0 shrank DB connection pool from 50 to 5, so checkout and api-gateway return 5xx errors
report.summary: Since 16:38Z, api-gateway has been returning 5xx errors on 7.5–32.5% of requests, and the rate is still climbing (32.5% at 16:44). Almost all of them are 502s passed up from checkout, and checkout's errors are 503s passed up from payments. payments v2.4.0 was deployed at 16:35Z ('Refactor DB client config loading'). It starts with pool.max_size=5 instead of 50, the pool sits at 5 of 5, and requests time out waiting for a DB connection. The fix is to roll payments back to v2.3.0.
report.impact: Public API traffic through api-gateway, which routes to checkout, which calls payments. Since 2026-10-26T16:38Z, api-gateway has failed between 7.5% and 32.5% of about 1000 requests per minute (18.4% over 5 minutes at alert time, 32.5% at 16:44). Its p95 latency went from about 180ms to 4.3–4.8s. Failed requests are failed order submissions and payment authorizations/captures. Inventory is not affected.

root_cause.hypothesis: The payments v2.4.0 refactor of DB client config loading set the Postgres connection pool to max_size=5 (v2.3.0 ran with 50, about 18 in use). The pool fills up, requests wait out the 3000ms timeout, and payments returns 503s. Checkout passes these up as 502s, and so does api-gateway. Postgres itself returned no metrics or logs, so I couldn't check it directly. Because payments is the side hitting its own cap of 5, the bottleneck looks client-side.
